Stephen Hughes
ste'ven hewz
n. (Stephen Hughes, 1622–1688, ejected Welsh minister, printer of Welsh Bibles and books)
Greek Stephanos, a crown; Welsh Hughes, son of Hugh.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Stephen Hughes was vicar of Meidrim in Carmarthenshire until the Act of Uniformity put him out in 1662, and he spent the remaining twenty-six years of his life getting Welsh books into Welsh hands. He collected and printed the verses of Rhys Prichard, saw editions of the Welsh Bible and New Testament through the London presses, published Welsh catechisms and a Welsh version of the first part of Pilgrim's Progress, and funded much of it by subscription from sympathetic gentry and merchants. He was called the Apostle of Carmarthenshire. The dictionary names him as the model of what an ejected minister may do when the pulpit is closed. Hughes could not preach legally; he could print, and he judged that a Bible in a farmhouse outlasts a sermon. The Welsh revival of the following century ran through districts saturated with the books he distributed, and he had been dead fifty years when it came.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines eject as to throw out and dispossess, and subscription as a sum subscribed toward a book or undertaking.

expand to see more

EJECT', v.t. To throw out; to cast forth; to dispossess of an office or benefice.

SUBSCRIP'TION, n. A paper to which names are subscribed; the sum subscribed toward the publication of a book.

DISTRIB'UTE, v.t. To divide among two or more; to deal out; to bestow in parts.

APOS'TLE, n. A person deputed to execute some important business; one of the twelve disciples of Christ.

Key Scripture

Ecc 11:1 — "Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days."

Ecc 11:6 — "In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that, or whether they both shall be alike good."

Psa 126:6 — "He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him."

Modern Corruption

Ejected in 1662, he spent twenty-six years printing Welsh Bibles and books instead of preaching.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a silenced minister's usefulness is over. Hughes lost the one thing he had been trained for and immediately found the second-best thing and did it for a quarter of a century, with results he never saw. Nonconformity in Wales was built far more on his distributed books than on any surviving pulpit.

The principle to recover is that the word is to be written and scattered, and that the sowing and the reaping are not in the same hand. “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables” (Hab 2:2). “Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days” (Ecc 11:1). The sowing is to continue without knowing which part will take: “In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand” (Ecc 11:6). And the promise to the man who sows weeping is kept, often long after him — “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him” (Psa 126:6).

Usage

"“Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables” (Hab 2:2) — Welsh Bibles through the London presses."

"“Cast thy bread upon the waters” (Ecc 11:1) — Prichard's verses collected and printed."

"“shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves” (Psa 126:6) — a revival he did not live to see."
